1	# Architecture
2	
3	Pre-read: [docs/vision.md](vision.md)
4	
5	Shipping a piece of agentic work is never one action — it is a sequence: code it, review it against the right standards, open the PR, make the description read well. A capable agent handles any one of these steps, one at a time, and driving each by hand holds up fine while the work is small. As the work grows more complex, that hand-driving breaks down — and what breaks reveals that the operator was holding three fused jobs together: the **state** (where the work stands), the **steps** (what runs, in what order, to what standard), and the **supervision** (moving each piece from one step to the next). Holding all three by hand carries two costs: execution quality swings with the operator's discipline on the day, and the operator must drive every transition by hand instead of planning the next work.
6	
7	So the question this architecture answers: how do you build the thing that holds the work together once — so the workflow runs the same way every time, without a person driving it — and how do the pieces of that system fit together?
8	
9	The answer is two layers over one shared record. **Layer 1 — supervision** (`drain-cycle`) drives the work and grades each result. **Layer 2 — workflow** (the Shaper pack) is the procedure itself, captured as composable skills. They meet at an **artifact boundary**: Layer 2 writes signals, Layer 1 reads them, and neither reaches inside the other. Both work off one **state plane** — a single authoritative record of where the work stands. The move that makes this real is small: `prompt.py` stops inlining the workflow and becomes a thin pointer at the workflow's front door, `exec:pickup`. The pack then owns the procedure, so any vendor's worker follows the same prose. The payoff removes both costs above — the workflow is captured once and a content-blind supervisor runs it unattended, so execution is consistent on every run instead of varying by the day, and the operator is needed only to point the system at planned work and to step in when a run halts.
10	
11	## 1. Split the work into two layers, one product
12	
13	The work splits into two layers:
14	
15	- **Layer 1 — supervision (`drain-cycle`).** Picks up a body of planned work and spawns a worker per phase per issue, holding the guardrails — halting, reverting, resuming, or recovering as the run demands. It then records and grades each outcome. It is vendor-agnostic: each worker is a `claude -p` (or any equivalent) subprocess.
16	- **Layer 2 — workflow (the Shaper pack).** The intra-issue procedure, captured as composable skills: how a piece of work goes from picked-up to merged PR. This is the knowledge that used to live in the operator's head, written down once.
17	
18	The vision's three pieces map onto this split: "one place for state" is the state plane (§7), "the steps become skills" is Layer 2, and "the supervision becomes a supervisor" is Layer 1.
19	
20	## 2. Layer 2 captures the workflow as composable skills
21	
22	The pack carries two types of skills:
23	
24	- **Planning — `shape:*`.**  `shape:idea`, `shape:project`, `shape:design`, `shape:delivery`. 
25	
26	- **Execution — `exec:*`.** 
27	  
28	  ```
29	  exec:pickup → exec:breakdown → exec:build → (exec:debug | exec:simplify)
30	              → exec:review → exec:verify → exec:finish
31	  ```
32	  
33	  `exec:pickup` is the front door; `exec:review` fans out reviewer personas; `exec:finish` is Graphite-first with a plain-git fallback and produces the trail artefacts (What/Why/Focus PR body, review-summary comment, Linear status move).
34	
35	Every step is also a standalone skill, so a human can run any one by hand. A **handoff envelope** carries the issue's acceptance criteria from pickup through to review, so the spec-compliance persona can grade *built-the-wrong-thing*, not just *built-it-badly*.
36	
37	## 3. Layer 1 owns process, not procedure
38	
39	`drain-cycle` owns process concerns only: spawn, guardrails, halt, revert, resume, recover, record, grade. It reads Linear state and the worker's artifacts to decide whether to advance to the next issue or stop. It does not contain workflow prose — the worker's prompt points at the entry skill and the procedure lives in Layer 2.
40	
41	The supervisor mechanics are documented in `docs/design-decisions.md`.
42	
43	## 4. Spawn a worker per phase, not per issue
44	
45	A worker does not run the whole `exec:*` chain. Each phase — code, review, finish — is its own spawn, with its own model tier, and the agent that produced an artifact never judges it. Two independent reasons force this:
46	
47	- **Independent verification.** A coder reviewing its own work rationalises its own choices. Spawning review as a separate agent that did not write the code makes review adversarial by construction, not by prompt wording.
48	- **Per-phase model economics.** Review anchors to a stronger (more expensive) model regardless of what coded the change. That asymmetry is only expressible if each phase is its own spawn with its own `--model` pin — a cheap model can build while an expensive one reviews.
49	
50	The three phase agents map onto the existing pack: code = `exec:build` (+`exec:debug`, `exec:simplify`), review = `exec:review`, finish = `exec:finish`. Each is a goal-shaped worker prompt, not a resident process — the goal ("produce sliced artifacts", "apply every quality lens", "land human-readable PRs") drives a sequence of skill delegations inside one spawn.
51	
52	The cost accepted in return: every phase boundary pays a spawn plus artifact rehydration, so the handoff envelope (§5) must carry everything the next phase needs — a single worker kept that context in memory for free. This is the deliberate price of independence; see design decision §20.
53	
54	## 5. Layer 2 writes signals; Layer 1 reads them
55	
56	The two layers meet at an artifact, not at a function call. **Layer 2 writes signals; Layer 1 reads them.** The supervisor never reads the workflow's steps — only the artifacts the workflow leaves behind: Linear issue state, run-log fields, and `.drain-handoff.json` (e.g. `pr_urls`).
57	
58	The placement test for any new behaviour: does `drain-cycle` need to know *what a role does* (Layer 2), or only *whether an artifact exists* (Layer 1)? Submitting a PR is "what a role does" — it belongs in a skill. Reading back the submitted PR URLs to decide whether to advance is "whether an artifact exists" — it belongs in the supervisor (see design decision §19).
59	
60	Keeping the boundary at the artifact is what makes Layer 1 content-blind, and content-blindness is what lets the same Layer 2 run under any worker.
61	
62	## 6. Dual-mode: the same skills by hand or unattended
63	
64	Because the workflow is skills and the supervisor only reads artifacts, the same skills run two ways: the operator invokes them at the keyboard, or a spawned worker runs them unattended. There is one workflow, exercised two ways — not a manual path and a separate automated path that drift apart.
65	
66	Design decision §10 (config symlinked into each worktree) is what makes the headless worker's environment match an interactive session, so a skill behaves the same in both modes.
67	
68	## 7. All state lives in one record — the state plane
69	
70	Everything works off one organized record of where the work stands. **Linear is authoritative** for issue status (design decision §1, §12). Beneath it sit the durable supervisor records: per-run logs (§4, §8), the atomic active-run marker (§11), and opt-in OpenTelemetry traces (§13).
71	
72	These records are the **delayed feedback loop** that replaces live watching. Automating supervision deliberately gives up the operator's real-time view of each worker; observability is how that trade is paid back. Better observability widens the set of work that is safe to hand off (§9).
73	
74	## 8. `prompt.py` becomes a pointer, not a script
75	
76	The move that realizes the whole split: **`prompt.py` becomes a thin pointer at `exec:pickup`** instead of inlining the workflow. The supervisor stops carrying procedure; the pack owns it; any vendor's worker follows the same prose. This is tracked by the "drain-cycle supervises; the pack owns the workflow" project and is the run-first step — everything else in this doc is a facet of it. Until it lands, the supervisor's prompt still names a few skills directly (e.g. the current `/code-review-and-quality` and `/shape:pr-finishing`); those references swap to `exec:*` at the keystone cutover.
77	
78	## 9. Extend the autonomy horizon as observability earns trust
79	
80	How far the supervisor runs without the operator. Today it drains a cycle transactionally — one issue, one worker, one diff — and halts when it runs out of runnable work or hits a result it cannot get past. The horizon extends outward as observability earns more trust: building on unmerged work, auto-merging trusted classes, and eventually a resident process that watches its own PRs through the review-and-merge loop. That extension is shaped in [`ideas/drain-past-the-merge-gate.md`](ideas/drain-past-the-merge-gate.md).
81	
82	The horizon is a deliberate trade, not a default: autonomy is applied selectively where the delayed feedback loop (§7) makes the loss of live intervention acceptable.
83	
84	## 10. From a one-shot CLI to a resident daemon
85	
86	The supervisor is moving from a one-shot CLI to a resident process — the autonomy horizon of §9 made concrete. Two scopes, both Layer 1:
87	
88	- **Control plane (one per machine).** The long-lived daemon. Owns process lifecycle, the queue of planned units to execute, and an API the operator queries and steers: what is running, halt this issue, resume, and (the horizon behaviour) watch open PRs through the review-and-merge loop and respond to review comments.
89	- **Execution-coordinator (one per unit in flight).** Spawned by the control plane to drive a single cycle or project. It advances work by reading artifacts (§5) — never by reading inside a phase — and halts on a missing or failed artifact.
90	
91	The control plane stays a **process, not a Claude skill** (design decision §22). A `/execute-cycle` skill would run inside a Claude session and collapse the artifact boundary that makes the worker vendor-agnostic; the one-command ergonomics come instead from a thin CLI front-door (`drain-cycle run <unit>`). "Respond to PR comments" is a control-plane behaviour, not a pack skill, because it requires watching a PR after it is open — which only a resident process does.
92	
93	## 11. Execute a planned unit — a cycle or a project
94	
95	The supervisor executes a *planned unit*. The atom is unchanged — one issue, with a worker per phase (§4) — and a cycle and a project differ only as containers with a hierarchy over them. "Drain a cycle" is one entry point, not the definition; project execution is out of scope today but is a later container, not a redesign (design decision §22). The tool keeps the name `drain-cycle`; the concept it serves is wider.
96	
97	## 12. Roll review up the tree: multi-altitude review
98	
99	`shape:delivery` decomposes committed work *downward* — project → milestones → nodes → tasks. Verification rolls *upward* along the same tree, with the review altitude matching the decomposition altitude:
100	
101	| Altitude             | Fires when                                   | Lenses                                                                                                                             |
102	| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
103	| **Task** (per issue) | a task's diff is ready, before its PR merges | spec-compliance · security · reliability/resilience · code-quality · outcome — diff-bounded                                        |
104	| **Milestone**        | a milestone's last child task lands          | integration/coherence/acceptance (the task lens raised a level) · regression (did landing degrade anything outside this boundary?) |
105	| **Project**          | a project's last milestone lands             | architecture review · measurable stated goals (partial — some goals take time and are deferred)                                    |
106	
107	Work fans down; verification rolls up. The trigger is structural — a parent's review fires exactly when its last child completes — and the hierarchy itself is authoritative in Linear (milestones, projects), so the state plane (§7) reads it rather than holding a second copy.
108	
109	Three consequences distinguish higher-altitude review from task review:
110	
111	1. **The execution-coordinator is a tree walker, not a queue drainer.** It models the hierarchy, detects "this milestone's last child landed", and fires the milestone review.
112	2. **Higher-altitude review produces new work, not reverts.** A task review can halt before a PR merges. A milestone or project review runs *after* its child PRs have merged — a merged slice cannot be cleanly reverted — so a failing review emits new remediation issues slotted back into the plan. This is a different halt semantic from task-level, and it widens the open seam below.
113	3. **Project review is partial and deferred.** Some goals cannot be measured at completion. Project review measures what it can now and *schedules* the rest, which is only possible with the resident control plane (§10).
114	
115	Two unknowns here are not yet decided and are shaped as spikes, not committed: the **blast-radius definition** for regression review (it is not diff-bounded like task review), and **remediation routing** (what gets created on a failing altitude review, and whether the parent pauses or its siblings keep draining). See design decision §21.
116	
117	## Decide the verdict-handoff schema before the correctness work
118	
119	The one undecided boundary crossing: how Layer-2 verdicts (`outcome_verdict`, `prep_verdict`) travel from a skill into the run-log. Today `handoff.py` carries only `pr_urls`. The verdict-handoff schema is a one-way door for the correctness work (the "Multi-agent collaboration for correctness" Layer-1 project) and should be decided before that work starts.
120	
121	The multi-altitude reviews (§12) widen this same seam: a milestone or project verdict has to cross the boundary too, and a failing one routes *remediation work* back into the plan rather than recording a pass/fail on a single diff. Whatever schema resolves the task-level verdict handoff should be designed to carry the higher-altitude verdicts as well.
122

1	# Architecture diagrams
2	
3	These diagrams illustrate [`../architecture.md`](../architecture.md). The committed `.svg` files are clean, first-pass renders that display on GitHub today. They are meant to be **redrawn in the hand-drawn Excalidraw aesthetic** later; this file is the label/layout spec to redraw from, so the wording stays 1:1 with the doc.
4	
5	**Rule that keeps the visuals honest:** the doc is authoritative. Every label here appears verbatim in `architecture.md`. Do not introduce friendlier or invented names when redrawing — if a term needs to change, change the doc first, then the diagram.
6	
7	## Diagram 1 — `architecture-overview.svg` (apex visual, after the lead)
8	
9	A top-to-bottom flow from the operator into the supervision layer, then into one planned unit, with review rolling back up.
10	
11	- **operator** → **Control plane (one per machine, resident daemon).** Layer 1. Owns process lifecycle and the queue of planned units; exposes a steer API (what's running · halt · resume); watches open PRs through the review-and-merge loop and responds to PR comments (horizon behaviour — only a resident process does this).
12	- Control plane **spawns one Execution-coordinator per unit in flight.** Layer 1, a tree walker. Advances work by reading artifacts (§5), never by reading inside a phase; halts on a missing or failed artifact.
13	- The coordinator drives one **planned unit**, drawn as nested containers: **PROJECT ⊃ MILESTONE ⊃ TASK (one issue).**
14	- Inside the task, three **phase spawns** run in sequence, each a Layer 2 skill:
15	  - `exec:build` — goal: produce sliced artifacts (+ `exec:debug`, `exec:simplify`)
16	  - `exec:review` — goal: apply every quality lens (fans out reviewer personas)
17	  - `exec:finish` — goal: land human-readable PRs (What/Why/Focus PR · summary comment · status move)
18	  - Annotate the build→review boundary: **"the agent that produced an artifact never judges it."**
19	- **Review altitudes** sit to the right, each aligned to its container:
20	  - **Task review** — diff-bounded, before the PR merges: spec-compliance · security · reliability/resilience · code-quality · outcome.
21	  - **Milestone review** — integration/coherence/acceptance · regression (outside this boundary); after child PRs merge → new work, not reverts.
22	  - **Project review** — architecture review · measurable stated goals (partial — some goals deferred).
23	- Edge arrows: **work fans down (decomposition)** on the left; **verification rolls up** on the right.
24	- Colour key: Layer 1 = blue, Layer 2 skills = green, review = amber.
25	
26	## Diagram 2 — `artifact-boundary.svg` (supports §5)
27	
28	Two stacked boxes with the boundary between them.
29	
30	- **Layer 2 — the workflow pack (skills)** on top: does the work, then leaves signals behind. **WRITES ↓.**
31	- **The artifact boundary** is a dashed line carrying three artifacts: **Linear issue state · run-log fields · `.drain-handoff.json` (`pr_urls`).**
32	- **Layer 1 — the supervisor** below: advances to the next issue, or halts, on whether an artifact exists. **READS ↓.**
33	- Caption: Layer 1 never reads the workflow's steps — only the artifacts it leaves behind; that content-blindness lets the same Layer 2 run under any worker.
34	
35	## Diagram 3 — multi-altitude review (deferred)
36	
37	Not drawn. The overview (Diagram 1) already shows the fan-down/roll-up duality and all three review altitudes, and `architecture.md` §12 carries the per-altitude lens table. Add a dedicated diagram only if a future reader finds the roll-up idea underserved by those two.
38

1	# Vision
2	
3	## Problem
4	
5	Doing a piece of work is never a single action. It's a sequence of steps - prompt an agent to write the code, review it against the right standards, open a PR, rewrite the PR description so a person can read it, and on from there. My agent handles any one of these steps well, but only one at a time, and only after I've set it up. Each step is its own conversation: I prompt it, refine what I mean, check what comes back.
6	
7	This holds up fine for small work. But the more complex the work gets - the more thinking and planning it needs up front - the faster that workflow breaks down. And when it breaks, it's clear the thing holding the work together was me all along, doing three jobs I'd never thought to separate:
8	
9	1. **Holding the state** - where the work stands: what's done, what's next, what's blocked. Ideally this lives in one organized place. By default, in agentic development, it scatters into loose markdown files that are painful to keep straight.
10	2. **Knowing the steps** - what the steps are, what order they run in, and the standard each one has to meet. That knowledge lives in my head and comes out a little differently every time.
11	3. **Supervising the run** - moving each piece of work from one step to the next, pushing a worker from "coding" to "reviewing" to "open the PR," kicking off each step, watching what comes back, and carrying on to the next.
12	
13	The last two feel like a single job, because I do them in the same breath - I drive the work and carry the process in my head at the same time, and never notice they're two different things.
14	
15	Carrying all three myself leaves me with two problems I can't get out from under:
16	
17	1. **Execution is inconsistent.** Because the steps live in my head, the care they get depends on me. On a good day I break the work down and run every step methodically. On a worse one I get lazy, skip a step, or forget part of the process - so the same kind of work gets a different level of care depending on the day.
18	2. **I'm pinned to supervising.** Because the driving eats my attention, I can't do much else while my workers run. I can't step back to think about the next set of projects or to level myself up.
19	
20	So the problem isn't doing the work. It's that holding it all together - the state, the steps, the supervision - falls entirely on me, and the more demanding the work, the worse that gets.
21	
22	## Solution
23	
24	The way out is to stop *being* the thing that holds the work together and build that thing once instead. It rests on three pieces, and they line up with the three things the problem dumps on me - the state, the steps, and the supervision.
25	
26	**One place for state.** Everything starts from a single, organized record of where the work stands: what's done, what's next, what's blocked. Instead of each piece of work's status scattering across loose markdown files, there's one source of truth, and everything else works off it. This is the ground the rest stands on. Of the three, state was the one I already treated as its own job. The other two I carried fused - knowing the work and supervising it, done in the same breath. Pulled apart, each becomes something I can build.
27	
28	**The steps become skills.** Knowing the work is knowing what the steps are, what order they run in, and what standard each one has to meet. That knowledge used to live in my head and come out a little differently every time. I capture it as skills: one skill per step, plus a sequence that runs them in order. The process is written down once, out in the open, the same on every run.
29	
30	**The supervision becomes a supervisor.** The other half is the mechanical part - kick off each step, watch it, check it produced what it should, move to the next, stop and flag anything it can't get past. That's pure mechanics, the part of me that isn't thinking. It gets automated into a supervisor - I call it the drain-cycle - that drives the skills, verifies each result, updates the record, and carries each piece of work along on its own. I'm no longer the connector between steps. I built the connector, and my job moves up a level: I point it at a body of planned work - a cycle now, a whole project later - and let it run.
31	
32	And because the work is planned as a hierarchy - a project holds milestones, a milestone holds tasks - the connector verifies at every altitude, not just the bottom. It checks each task as it lands, then checks each milestone once its tasks are in (did the pieces cohere, did landing them break anything outside their boundary), then checks the project against the goals that can be measured by the end. The connector verifies up the same hierarchy it broke the work down along.
33	
34	**Before - I am the connector**
35	
36	```
37	me     → "write the code for this"
38	agent  → writes it
39	me     → read it. "now review it against these standards"
40	agent  → reviews it
41	me     → "open a PR"
42	agent  → opens it
43	me     → "rewrite the PR description so it reads well"
44	agent  → rewrites it
45	me     → check it, mark it done
46	       → then start the whole chain over for the next piece of work
47	```
48	
49	I'm there at every arrow - for every piece of work in the project. And on a tired day, I skip one.
50	
51	**After - I built the connector**
52	
53	```
54	me         → "work through this project"
55	supervisor → picks up the first piece of work
56	           → runs build → review → PR → finish, checking each result
57	           → marks it done, moves to the next
58	           → ...
59	           → hits one it can't get past review, stops, tells me why
60	me         → review the finished work; step in only where it halted
61	```
62	
63	I'm there once at the start, and again only when something genuinely needs me.
64	
65	**What changes for me**
66	
67	Two things.
68	
69	First, the work gets *more consistent than I am.* Because the steps are captured once and the supervisor runs them the same way every time, execution stops depending on my discipline. It doesn't get tired, skip a step, or forget the process on a bad day, so every piece of work gets the same level of care, not whatever level I happened to have that afternoon.
70	
71	Second, my attention comes off the mechanical loop entirely. Instead of walking each piece of work through the same chain of steps, I move to the work that needs a person: scoping the next project, judging whether finished work is any good, and improving the system itself.
72	
73	And this pays off hardest exactly where the problem hurt most. The more complex the work (the more steps, the more planning) the more the old way leaned on me and the more it broke down. The new way leans on the same captured process and the same supervisor no matter how big the project gets.
74	
```

# Plan — Render `docs/architecture.md` as a reader-optimized HTML page

## Context

`docs/architecture.md` is the project's architecture doc. The owner wants a standalone HTML page to become the **primary** way the architecture is shown — the markdown will be deleted once the HTML reads/looks right. So this is not a faithful 1:1 transcode: the brief is to "optimize 100% for the reader" and re-examine the structure with fresh eyes.

Reading the doc fresh, its 12 flat numbered sections fall into three natural acts, each answering one reader question. Regrouping them gives the page a narrative spine without changing the (already tight, authoritative) prose. Two committed SVG diagrams exist but are light-mode-only; rebuilding them as native themeable HTML/CSS makes them crisp and dark-mode aware. The repo already has a house HTML style (the `shape:render-html` template) in `docs/initiative-multi-agent-collaboration.html` and `docs/integration-test-architecture.html` — the new page should match it for consistency.

**Decisions locked with the owner:**
1. **Regroup into 3 acts** (keep original §-numbers as anchors so cross-refs resolve).
2. **Rebuild both diagrams as native HTML/CSS** (labels verbatim per `docs/images/README.md`).
3. **Add light scaffolding** — per-act TL;DR, vision three-pieces mapping callout, before/after operator diagrams from `vision.md` — but **no prose rewriting**.

## Output

Single self-contained file: **`docs/architecture.html`** (no external assets — diagrams are inline HTML/CSS, not `<img>`). Self-contained matches the two existing rendered HTML docs in `docs/` and keeps the page portable once the `.md` is gone.

## Source of truth

- Prose: `docs/architecture.md` — copy verbatim into the relevant act. Do not reword.
- Diagram labels: `docs/images/README.md` is the label spec; every label appears verbatim in `architecture.md`. Do not invent friendlier names.
- Borrowed scaffolding: `docs/vision.md` (three pieces §"Solution"; before/after operator blocks lines 34–63).

## House style to reuse

Lift the `<style>` block and page chrome from `docs/initiative-multi-agent-collaboration.html` (lines 7–120+):
- CSS custom-property theme tokens incl. `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`.
- `--accent` (Layer-... neutral), plus map the diagram color key onto existing tokens: **Layer 1 = `--info`/`--info-soft` (blue)**, **Layer 2 skills = `--ok`/`--ok-soft` (green)**, **review = `--warn`/`--warn-soft` (amber)** — these already exist and have dark-mode variants.
- Sticky sidebar nav, `.doc-head`, `section.s` headers, `.pill`, `.meta-grid`, `<pre>` styling, scroll-spy active-link JS if present in the template.

## Page structure

**Doc header** — title "Architecture", subtitle = the one-line SCQ-A answer ("Two layers over one shared record…"), breadcrumb/pre-read link to `vision.md`. Pill row: `drain-cycle` · Layer 1 / Layer 2.

**Lead** — the SCQ-A opening (architecture.md lines 5–9) verbatim. Follow with the **apex diagram** (rebuilt `architecture-overview.svg` as HTML/CSS) and a **callout** mapping the vision's three pieces → this architecture (one place for state → state plane §7; steps become skills → Layer 2; supervision becomes supervisor → Layer 1).

**Act I — The split: two layers, one record** (TL;DR one-liner)
- §1 Split into two layers, one product
- §2 Layer 2 captures the workflow as composable skills — render the `exec:*` chain as a styled `<pre>`/pipeline strip
- §3 Layer 1 owns process, not procedure
- §7 All state lives in one record — the state plane

**Act II — How the layers meet** (TL;DR one-liner)
- §5 Layer 2 writes signals; Layer 1 reads them — rebuilt **artifact-boundary** diagram (HTML/CSS) inline here
- §4 Spawn a worker per phase, not per issue — the two reasons (independent verification, per-phase model economics) as a two-card block
- §6 Dual-mode: the same skills by hand or unattended — optionally fold in the `vision.md` before/after operator blocks as the human-readable face of dual-mode
- §8 `prompt.py` becomes a pointer — flag visually as **the keystone** (callout treatment)

**Act III — How far it runs** (TL;DR one-liner)
- §9 Extend the autonomy horizon as observability earns trust
- §10 From a one-shot CLI to a resident daemon — control plane vs execution-coordinator as a two-column compare
- §11 Execute a planned unit — a cycle or a project
- §12 Roll review up the tree — the altitude table as a proper styled `<table>`; fan-down/roll-up duality called out

**Closing — Open decision** — "Decide the verdict-handoff schema before the correctness work" as a distinct amber/warn callout, not a numbered section (it's an open question, not settled architecture).

Each section keeps an `id="s4"` style anchor (matching its original §-number) plus a slug, so any external links to "§N" still resolve.

## Diagram rebuild notes (native HTML/CSS)

- **Overview** (`architecture-overview.svg`): vertical flow operator → Control plane → Execution-coordinator → nested PROJECT ⊃ MILESTONE ⊃ TASK; inside TASK the three phase cards `exec:build` → `exec:review` → `exec:finish` with the "the agent that produced an artifact never judges it" annotation on the build→review edge; review-altitude cards (Task/Milestone/Project) aligned right; "work fans down" / "verification rolls up" rail labels; color legend. Use nested fl/grid `<div>`s with dashed borders for the containers, the three token colors, and a small legend row. All label text verbatim.
- **Artifact boundary** (`artifact-boundary.svg`): Layer 2 card (green, "WRITES ↓") on top → dashed boundary carrying three artifact chips (`Linear issue state` · `run-log fields` · `.drain-handoff.json (pr_urls)`) → Layer 1 card (blue, "READS ↓") below, with the two-line content-blindness caption.
- Keep diagrams responsive: stack/scroll gracefully under ~720px width.

## Build approach

1. Read the full `<style>` + chrome from `docs/initiative-multi-agent-collaboration.html` to lift the template exactly (only ~120 lines read so far).
2. Write `docs/architecture.html` in one pass: head/style → sidebar nav (3 acts) → doc header → lead + apex diagram + three-pieces callout → Act I/II/III sections (prose verbatim) → closing callout.
3. Add the two diagram component styles + the pipeline strip + the altitude table.

## Verification

- Open `docs/architecture.html` in a browser (or Chrome DevTools MCP) and confirm:
  - Renders with no console errors; sidebar nav anchors jump correctly; scroll-spy (if lifted) highlights the active section.

- Diff-read the prose against `architecture.md` to confirm nothing was reworded or dropped (all 12 §-anchors present + closing).

185	      <h1>Integration test architecture</h1>
186	      <div class="pill-row"></div>
187	      <dl class="meta-grid">
188	        <dt>Linear initiative</dt><dd><a href="https://linear.app/ababushkin/project/test-drain-cycle-failure-modes-and-resume-without-a-real-linear-cycle-910b954af13f">Test drain-cycle failure modes and resume without a real Linear cycle</a></dd>
189	        <dt>Source</dt><dd>docs/integration-test-architecture.md</dd>
190	        <dt>Rendered</dt><dd>2026-05-28</dd>
191	      </dl>
192	    </div>
193	
194	    <div class="preamble">
195	      <p>The OKR (Goal + Key Results + appetite + kill condition) is on the Linear project. This doc is the design — what gets built, why, in what order — and is the input to <code>shape-planning-and-task-breakdown</code> when the initiative is sliced into issues.</p>
196	    </div>
197	
198	    <section class="s" id="context">
199	      <header><span class="ix">01</span><h2>Context</h2></header>
200	      <p>Today <code>drain-cycle</code> only tests against a real Linear cycle. Anything past happy-path becomes expensive: failure modes need deliberately broken issues, resume needs an actual halt-and-restart, and usage tracking needs real Claude sessions. Unit tests cover individual modules but stop at the function boundary — they monkey-patch <code>linear._post</code> and swap <code>claude -p</code> for marker-touching shell scripts (<code>tests/test_orchestrator_iteration.py:22</code>, <code>tests/test_linear_pending_issues.py:65</code>).</p>
201	      <p>We need <strong>scenario-level integration tests</strong> that drive the orchestrator end-to-end against a controllable Linear surface, covering:</p>
202	      <ul>
203	        <li><strong>Best-case drains</strong> — dependency-ordered execution, runlog shape, state transitions</li>
204	        <li><strong>Per-issue failure paths</strong> — every halt condition in <code>orchestrator._drain_one_issue</code> (repo resolution, worktree setup, <code>set_state</code> failure, breach kill, not-Done exit)</li>
205	        <li><strong>Cycle-level halts</strong> — <code>DependencyCycleError</code>, cycle-cap breach propagation</li>
206	        <li><strong>Resume semantics</strong> — halt mid-cycle, re-run, observe pickup of in-flight issues reverted to Todo</li>
207	        <li><strong>Session/usage tracking</strong> — <code>_UsageAccumulator</code> totals, cycle aggregates in runlog, per-issue caps triggering breaches</li>
208	      </ul>
209	      <p>The drain has no native retry (deliberate, per <code>docs/design-decisions.md</code>); "retry" here means <strong>resume</strong> — a re-invocation against the same cycle.</p>
210	    </section>
211

213	      <header><span class="ix">02</span><h2>System context</h2></header>
214	      <p>The seam choice in one picture: real <code>claude -p</code>, mocked Linear, glued by an MCP shim that translates child MCP calls into GraphQL against the same in-memory store the parent hits over HTTP.</p>

286	        <p class="p-diagram-caption">Solid = control / data flow over HTTP or subprocess. Dashed (accent) = MCP stdio between the child and the shim. The dashed boundary marks what's mocked: every byte that would otherwise hit <code>api.linear.app</code> is intercepted, but <code>claude -p</code> itself is the production binary every run. 290	    <section class="s" id="workflow">
291	      <header><span class="ix">03</span><h2>Workflow</h2></header>
292	      <ol>
293	        <li><strong><code>/shape-initiative</code></strong> — done. Linear project created with the six-field OKR (linked above).</li>
294	        <li><strong><code>shape-planning-and-task-breakdown</code></strong> — convert the <em>Slices</em> section below into Linear issues under the new initiative; assign slices 1–4 to the current cycle, 5–12 to the backlog.</li>
295	        <li><strong><code>agent-skills:test-driven-development</code></strong> during build — each slice ships a failing scenario before the supporting infra.</li>
296	        <li><strong><code>agent-skills:code-review-and-quality</code></strong> per slice before commit, per <code>AGENTS.md</code>.</li>
297	      </ol>
298	    </section>
299	
300	    <section class="s" id="approach">
301	      <header><span class="ix">04</span><h2>Approach</h2></header>
302	      <p><strong>Parent HTTP mock + Linear-MCP shim + real <code>claude -p</code> + in-process driver.</strong> The spawned session is real claude every time; only the Linear surface is mocked. Three pillars.</p>
303	      <p><strong>Alternatives rejected</strong> (draft for the ADR slice):</p>
304	      <ul>
305	        <li><strong>Scripted/fake <code>claude -p</code>.</strong> Cheaper, faster, deterministic. Rejected because a scripted child stops being an integration test — it cannot validate the real session's usage stream, MCP tool calls, prompt-to-completion behaviour, or production OTel spans against actual data.</li>
306	        <li><strong>Hybrid: real claude only on happy-path; scripted child for failure determinism.</strong> Two patterns to maintain; weaker default signal; gives up real-claude coverage on usage-tracking edge cases.</li>
307	        <li><strong>Function-injection / <code>LinearClient</code> protocol on the parent.</strong> Cheaper than HTTP but skips the HTTP boundary and adds an abstraction layer that earns nothing else. The existing module-level functions in <code>linear.py</code> drive easily against an HTTP fake once <code>LINEAR_API_URL</code> is overridable.</li>
308	        <li><strong>VCR-style recorded fixtures.</strong> Realistic but awkward for failure injection, expensive to maintain under schema drift.</li>
309	      </ul>
310	      <p>Slice 1 produces a short ADR at <code>docs/adrs/0001-integration-test-architecture.md</code> recording the chosen approach, these rejected alternatives, and revisit conditions.</p>
311	
312	      <h3 id="cost-runtime-and-determinism">Cost, runtime, and determinism</h3>
313	      <p>Real claude makes the suite costly, slow, and non-deterministic on numbers.</p>
314	      <ul>
315	        <li><strong>Cost / runtime budget</strong>: ~$0.05–$0.20 per spawning scenario, ~15–30 seconds per scenario. Full suite of ~30 scenarios: ~$1–$3 and ~15 minutes. Run on demand, not as part of the default suite.</li>
316	        <li><strong>Default <code>pytest</code> run</strong> covers only the pre-spawn halt scenarios (no claude spawned) — fast and deterministic, suitable for repeated local invocation while iterating.</li>
317	        <li><strong>Determinism strategy</strong> — split assertions:
318	          <ul>
319	            <li><strong>Exact</strong> — exit codes, final Linear state, halt reason class, runlog file presence, structural shape of runlog JSON, set of MCP tool calls observed.</li>
320	            <li><strong>Predicate</strong> — <code>tokens &gt; 0</code>, <code>0 &lt; cost_usd &lt; per_issue_cost_usd</code>, <code>num_turns &gt;= 1</code>, <code>model is not None</code>. No exact values.</li>
321	            <li><strong>Tolerant snapshot</strong> — <code>dirty-equals</code> matches keys and types, ignores values.</li>
322	          </ul>
323	        </li>
324	        <li><strong>Cost guard</strong>: scenarios that spawn claude carry <code>@pytest.mark.real_claude</code>. Default <code>pytest</code> invocation excludes the marker; the <code>real_claude</code> slice opts in via <code>pytest -m real_claude</code> and runs on demand. <code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY</code> required.</li>
325	      </ul>
326	
327	      <h3 id="pillar-1-mocklinear">Pillar 1 — <code>MockLinear</code>: an in-process fake GraphQL server</h3>
328	      <p>A FastAPI/Starlette app on a random localhost port, started per-test via a pytest fixture. It speaks the five GraphQL operations <code>linear.py</code> uses (<code>current_cycle</code>, <code>pending_issues</code>, <code>get_issue</code>, <code>set_state</code>, <code>resolve_state</code> / WorkflowState lookup) plus an <code>IssueUpdate</code> mutation the scripted child hits to flip an issue to Done.</p>
329	      <p>State lives in a typed in-memory store: <code>Cycle</code>, <code>Issue</code>, <code>Label</code>, <code>WorkflowState</code>. The store records every call (operation, variables, timestamp) so tests can assert call sequence and counts.</p>
330	      <p>Fault injection is <strong>per-operation, per-call-index</strong>: <code>mock.fail_after(op="set_state", call=2, mode="http_500")</code>. Modes: <code>http_500</code>, <code>http_429</code>, <code>graphql_error</code>, <code>malformed_json</code>, <code>slow_response(seconds)</code>, <code>connection_reset</code>. The drain has no retry, so "fail" means "this single call breaks" — tests then verify the halt path.</p>
331	      <p><strong>Production change required</strong>: <code>linear.py:18</code> hard-codes <code>https://api.linear.app/graphql</code>. Replace with <code>os.environ.get("LINEAR_API_URL", "https://api.linear.app/graphql")</code>. No CLI flag — env var only.</p>
332	
333	      <h3 id="pillar-2-linear-mcp-shim">Pillar 2 — <code>linear_mcp_shim</code>: a Linear MCP server backed by the mock</h3>
334	      <p>A small Python stdio MCP server (built on the official <code>mcp</code> SDK) that exposes the two tools the drain-cycle prompt uses today: <code>save_issue</code> (state transitions) and <code>save_comment</code>. Each tool translates its call into a GraphQL POST against <code>MockLinear</code>, sharing the same backing store as the parent's HTTP surface.</p>
335	      <p>The harness writes a custom <code>.mcp.json</code> into each test worktree registering the shim under the name <code>linear</code> (matching the existing tool prefix <code>mcp__claude_ai_Linear__*</code>). The orchestrator already symlinks <code>.mcp.json</code> from the configured source into the worktree (<code>orchestrator.py:257-259</code>); the harness arranges for the test source to be the shim-configured file.</p>
336	      <p>The shim records every tool call (tool name, arguments, timestamp) on the shared store, so scenarios assert against both parent GraphQL calls and child MCP calls through one call log.</p>
337	      <p><strong>Why an MCP shim and not just <code>LINEAR_API_URL</code> in the child env.</strong> MCP is a separate protocol from raw GraphQL; the official Linear MCP server speaks MCP over stdio to claude and HTTPS to Linear. Setting <code>LINEAR_API_URL</code> in the child has no effect — there's no way to redirect the official server without forking it. A purpose-built shim is the smallest seam.</p>
338

413	      <h3 id="how-scenarios-steer-claude">How scenarios steer claude</h3>
414	      <p>Scenarios drive child behaviour through three knobs the harness sets per-scenario:</p>
415	      <ul>
416	        <li><strong>Issue body</strong> — written into <code>MockLinear</code> and read by claude via <code>mcp__claude_ai_Linear__get_issue</code>. The body is the natural prompt seam (e.g. "create <code>&lt;id&gt;.txt</code> containing 'hello'; then mark this issue Done"). Library lives in <code>tests/integration/prompts/*.md</code>.</li>
417	        <li><strong>Per-issue limits</strong> — <code>limits.yml</code> overrides (e.g. <code>per_issue_tokens=2000</code>, <code>per_issue_seconds=30</code>) used with verbose prompts to provoke breach scenarios deterministically.</li>
418	        <li><strong>Claude flags</strong> — the harness may inject <code>--max-turns 1</code> for "exit without Done" cases (claude exits before completing the workflow), via the <code>_CLAUDE_CMD</code> patch point at <code>orchestrator.py:25</code>.</li>
419	      </ul>
420	      <p>The drain-cycle prompt (<code>drain_cycle/prompt.py:39-42</code>) stays unchanged — same prompt the real drain uses.</p>
421	
422	      <h3 id="pillar-3-integrationharness">Pillar 3 — <code>IntegrationHarness</code>: a fixture that drives <code>orchestrator.run()</code> in-process</h3>
423	      <p>A pytest fixture that:</p>
424	      <ul>
425	        <li>Creates a temp <code>HOME</code> so <code>~/.drain-cycle/repos.yml</code>, <code>~/.drain-cycle/limits.yml</code>, and <code>~/.drain-cycle/runs/</code> redirect to a tmpdir (<code>monkeypatch.setenv("HOME", ...)</code> plus any path-resolution helpers in <code>cli.py</code> / <code>runlog.py</code>).</li>
426	        <li>Initialises one or more real git repos in tmpdir (existing pattern in <code>test_orchestrator_iteration.py</code>).</li>
427	        <li>Writes a <code>repos.yml</code> mapping label names to those repo paths.</li>
428	        <li>Writes a <code>.mcp.json</code> in each repo registering the Linear-MCP shim under <code>linear</code>.</li>
429	        <li>Starts <code>MockLinear</code> and populates it with the scenario's cycle, issues (with prompt body), and labels.</li>
430	        <li>Sets <code>LINEAR_API_URL</code>, <code>LINEAR_API_KEY=test</code>, <code>MOCK_LINEAR_URL=http://localhost:&lt;port&gt;</code>, <code>OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true</code> env vars. Verifies <code>ANTHROPIC_API_KEY</code> is set for scenarios that spawn claude.</li>
431	        <li>Optionally appends extra flags to <code>_CLAUDE_CMD</code> (e.g. <code>--max-turns 1</code>) for scenarios that need to coerce claude's behaviour.</li>
432	        <li>Calls <code>orchestrator.run(repos, limits)</code> directly and returns a <code>Result</code>: exit code, runlog JSON, parent GraphQL call log, child MCP call log, final mock state.</li>
433	      </ul>
434	      <p>Tests assert against <code>Result</code>. One scenario per <code>test_*</code> function. Helpers (<code>make_cycle</code>, <code>make_issue</code>, <code>expect_runlog</code>, <code>expect_calls</code>) keep scenarios short.</p>
435	      <p><strong>Per-scenario contract.</strong> Every scenario declares:</p>
436	      <ol>
437	        <li><strong>Setup</strong> — <code>Cycle</code>, <code>Issue[]</code>, <code>Label[]</code>, <code>WorkflowState[]</code>, repos.yml mapping, limits.yml overrides, transcript fixture name(s), any fault injection.</li>
438	        <li><strong>Expected exit code</strong> — orchestrator return.</li>
439	        <li><strong>Expected runlog assertions</strong> — a list of (a) structural shape (keys, types) matched via <code>dirty-equals</code>, (b) predicate assertions on numeric fields (<code>tokens &gt; 0</code>, <code>cost_usd &lt; limits.per_issue_cost_usd</code>), (c) exact assertions on deterministic fields (<code>final_linear_state</code>, <code>halt_reason</code>).</li>
440	        <li><strong>Expected final mock state</strong> — issue states the mock should end in (e.g. <code>{ "ABA-1": "Done", "ABA-2": "Todo" }</code> after a halt on issue 2).</li>
441	        <li><strong>Expected call sequence</strong> — ordered <code>(surface, operation, predicate-on-args)</code> tuples across both parent GraphQL and child MCP calls. Strict by default; <code>expect_calls(strict=False)</code> for tolerant cases where claude's tool-call order varies between runs.</li>
442	      </ol>
443	      <p>A collection-time lint test fails any scenario missing (3), (4), or (5).</p>
444	    </section>
445	
446	    <section class="s" id="production-code-changes-required">
447	      <header><span class="ix">05</span><h2>Production code changes required</h2></header>
448	      <p>Minimal. Every test-only seam reuses existing structure.</p>
449	      <ol>
450	        <li><strong><code>drain_cycle/linear.py:18</code></strong> — <code>_GRAPHQL_URL</code> reads from <code>LINEAR_API_URL</code> env var, default unchanged. One-line change.</li>
451	        <li><strong><code>drain_cycle/runlog.py</code></strong> — verify the run-log directory honours <code>HOME</code> re-resolution; slice 1 greps for <code>Path.home</code>, <code>expanduser</code>, and <code>HOME</code>. If the path caches at module load, add an accessor (e.g. <code>_run_log_dir()</code>) so the harness re-resolves after <code>monkeypatch.setenv("HOME", ...)</code>.</li>
452	        <li><strong><code>drain_cycle/orchestrator.py:25</code></strong> — <code>_CLAUDE_CMD</code> is already module-level. Tests patch it.</li>
453	      </ol>
454	      <p>No new abstraction layers, no <code>LinearClient</code> Protocol — the existing module-level functions drive easily against an HTTP fake once the URL is configurable.</p>
455	    </section>
456	
457	    <section class="s" id="test-infra-correctness-checks">
458	      <header><span class="ix">06</span><h2>Test-infra correctness checks (one-time pre-slice work)</h2></header>
459	      <p>Risks the plan-review surfaced. Each lands before dependent slices.</p>
460	      <ul>
461	        <li><strong>Telemetry isolation</strong> — drain-cycle wires httpx OTel auto-instrumentation in <code>telemetry.py</code>. The harness sets <code>OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true</code> to keep tests from exporting spans. Confirmed in slice 2.</li>
462	        <li><strong>MCP-shim correctness</strong> — the shim must implement the same tool schemas the official Linear MCP exposes for <code>save_issue</code> and <code>save_comment</code>, otherwise claude's tool calls land with wrong shapes. Slice 3 spike: capture the official schemas (from the Linear MCP docs or by running the real one briefly), implement matching ones in the shim, verify a single happy-path drain reaches Done end-to-end. <strong>Kill-switch</strong>: if the schemas drift between Linear MCP versions, pin the shim to a captured snapshot and add a periodic check.</li>
463	        <li><strong>Breach scenario reproducibility</strong> — with real claude, breach scenarios depend on prompts that reliably exceed tight per-issue caps. Slice 8 spike: confirm a verbose prompt (e.g. "write a 2000-line poem") plus <code>per_issue_tokens=1000</code> reliably triggers token breach across 5 consecutive runs. <strong>Kill-switch</strong>: if not reliable, fall back to time-breach only (tight <code>per_issue_seconds</code> plus a "sleep 60s" prompt is robust because the breach loop polls wall-clock).</li>
464	      </ul>
465	    </section>

491	
492	    <section class="s" id="scenario-catalogue">
493	      <header><span class="ix">08</span><h2>Scenario catalogue (initial coverage)</h2></header>
494	      <p>Grouped by area; one test function each. Target end-state, not a single slice — slices below build the infra and add scenarios incrementally.</p>
495	      <p>Scenarios that spawn <code>claude -p</code> carry <code>@pytest.mark.real_claude</code> (excluded from the default <code>pytest</code> run; opt-in via <code>-m real_claude</code>). Scenarios that halt pre-spawn run on every default invocation.</p>
496	
497	      <p><strong>Best case</strong> <em>(real_claude)</em></p>
498	      <ul>
499	        <li>3-issue dependency-ordered drain reaches Done in order; runlog totals positive and sum across issues; child MCP calls include <code>save_issue</code> (transition to Done) and <code>save_comment</code> (summary) per issue</li>
500	        <li>Mixed Todo + Backlog states picked up; correct planning</li>
501	        <li>Single-issue drain</li>
502	        <li>Empty cycle exits cleanly <em>(no claude spawned)</em></li>
503	      </ul>
504	
505	      <p><strong>Per-issue halts</strong> (<code>orchestrator._drain_one_issue</code> paths)</p>
506	      <ul>
507	        <li>Missing <code>repo:</code> label → halt + reason <em>(no claude spawned)</em></li>
508	        <li><code>repo:</code> label resolves to nonexistent path → halt <em>(no claude spawned)</em></li>
509	        <li>Worktree <code>add</code> fails (dirty tree) → halt <em>(no claude spawned)</em></li>
510	        <li><code>set_state</code> (Todo→In-Progress) fails with HTTP 500 → halt <em>(no claude spawned)</em></li>

516	      </ul>

521	        <li>After two Done issues, cycle-cap breach detected → third issue not attempted; halt reason names cumulative metric <em>(real_claude)</em></li>

527	      </ul>

534	      </ul>

539	      </ul>

Plan accordingly: keep the dedup unit test (<code>test_usage_accumulator_dedup.py</code> or equivalent); the integration suite asserts on monotonicity, not on dedup directly.</p>

1	# Vision
2	
3	## Problem
4	
5	Doing a piece of work is never a single action. It's a sequence of steps - prompt an agent to write the code, review it against the right standards, open a PR, rewrite the PR description so a person can read it, and on from there. My agent handles any one of these steps well, but only one at a time, and only after I've set it up. Each step is its own conversation: I prompt it, refine what I mean, check what comes back.
6	
7	This holds up fine for small work. But the more complex the work gets - the more thinking and planning it needs up front - the faster that workflow breaks down. And when it breaks, it's clear the thing holding the work together was me all along, doing three jobs I'd never thought to separate:
8	
9	1. **Holding the state** - where the work stands: what's done, what's next, what's blocked. Ideally this lives in one organized place. By default, in agentic development, it scatters into loose markdown files that are painful to keep straight.
10	2. **Knowing the steps** - what the steps are, what order they run in, and the standard each one has to meet. That knowledge lives in my head and comes out a little differently every time.
11	3. **Supervising the run** - moving each piece of work from one step to the next, pushing a worker from "coding" to "reviewing" to "open the PR," kicking off each step, watching what comes back, and carrying on to the next.
12	
13	The last two feel like a single job, because I do them in the same breath - I drive the work and carry the process in my head at the same time, and never notice they're two different things.
14	
15	Carrying all three myself leaves me with two problems I can't get out from under:
16	
17	1. **Execution is inconsistent.** Because the steps live in my head, the care they get depends on me. On a good day I break the work down and run every step methodically. On a worse one I get lazy, skip a step, or forget part of the process - so the same kind of work gets a different level of care depending on the day.
18	2. **I'm pinned to supervising.** Because the driving eats my attention, I can't do much else while my workers run. I can't step back to think about the next set of projects or to level myself up.
19	
20	So the problem isn't doing the work. It's that holding it all together - the state, the steps, the supervision - falls entirely on me, and the more demanding the work, the worse that gets.
21	
22	## Solution
23	
24	The way out is to stop *being* the thing that holds the work together and build that thing once instead. It rests on three pieces, and they line up with the three things the problem dumps on me - the state, the steps, and the supervision.
25	
26	**One place for state.** Everything starts from a single, organized record of where the work stands: what's done, what's next, what's blocked. Instead of each piece of work's status scattering across loose markdown files, there's one source of truth, and everything else works off it. This is the ground the rest stands on. Of the three, state was the one I already treated as its own job. The other two I carried fused - knowing the work and supervising it, done in the same breath. Pulled apart, each becomes something I can build.
27	
28	**The steps become skills.** Knowing the work is knowing what the steps are, what order they run in, and what standard each one has to meet. That knowledge used to live in my head and come out a little differently every time. I capture it as skills: one skill per step, plus a sequence that runs them in order. The process is written down once, out in the open, the same on every run.
29	
30	**The supervision becomes a supervisor.** The other half is the mechanical part - kick off each step, watch it, check it produced what it should, move to the next, stop and flag anything it can't get past. That's pure mechanics, the part of me that isn't thinking. It gets automated into a supervisor - I call it the drain-cycle - that drives the skills, verifies each result, updates the record, and carries each piece of work along on its own. I'm no longer the connector between steps. I built the connector, and my job moves up a level: I point it at a body of planned work - a cycle now, a whole project later - and let it run.
31	
32	And because the work is planned as a hierarchy - a project holds milestones, a milestone holds tasks - the connector verifies at every altitude, not just the bottom. It checks each task as it lands, then checks each milestone once its tasks are in (did the pieces cohere, did landing them break anything outside their boundary), then checks the project against the goals that can be measured by the end. The connector verifies up the same hierarchy it broke the work down along.
33	
34	**Before - I am the connector**
35	
36	```
37	me     → "write the code for this"
38	agent  → writes it
39	me     → read it. "now review it against these standards"
40	agent  → reviews it
41	me     → "open a PR"
42	agent  → opens it
43	me     → "rewrite the PR description so it reads well"
44	agent  → rewrites it
45	me     → check it, mark it done
46	       → then start the whole chain over for the next piece of work
47	```
48	
49	I'm there at every arrow - for every piece of work in the project. And on a tired day, I skip one.
50	
51	**After - I built the connector**
52	
53	```
54	me         → "work through this project"
55	supervisor → picks up the first piece of work
56	           → runs build → review → PR → finish, checking each result
57	           → marks it done, moves to the next
58	           → ...
59	           → hits one it can't get past review, stops, tells me why
60	me         → review the finished work; step in only where it halted
61	```
62	
63	I'm there once at the start, and again only when something genuinely needs me.
64	
65	**What changes for me**
66	
67	Two things.
68	
69	First, the work gets *more consistent than I am.* Because the steps are captured once and the supervisor runs them the same way every time, execution stops depending on my discipline. It doesn't get tired, skip a step, or forget the process on a bad day, so every piece of work gets the same level of care, not whatever level I happened to have that afternoon.
70	
71	Second, my attention comes off the mechanical loop entirely. Instead of walking each piece of work through the same chain of steps, I move to the work that needs a person: scoping the next project, judging whether finished work is any good, and improving the system itself.
72	
73	And this pays off hardest exactly where the problem hurt most. The more complex the work (the more steps, the more planning) the more the old way leaned on me and the more it broke down. The new way leans on the same captured process and the same supervisor no matter how big the project gets.
74

1	# Architecture diagrams
2	
3	These diagrams illustrate [`../architecture.md`](../architecture.md). The committed `.svg` files are clean, first-pass renders that display on GitHub today. They are meant to be **redrawn in the hand-drawn Excalidraw aesthetic** later; this file is the label/layout spec to redraw from, so the wording stays 1:1 with the doc.
4	
5	**Rule that keeps the visuals honest:** the doc is authoritative. Every label here appears verbatim in `architecture.md`. Do not introduce friendlier or invented names when redrawing — if a term needs to change, change the doc first, then the diagram.
6	
7	## Diagram 1 — `architecture-overview.svg` (apex visual, after the lead)
8	
9	A top-to-bottom flow from the operator into the supervision layer, then into one planned unit, with review rolling back up.
10	
11	- **operator** → **Control plane (one per machine, resident daemon).** Layer 1. Owns process lifecycle and the queue of planned units; exposes a steer API (what's running · halt · resume); watches open PRs through the review-and-merge loop and responds to PR comments (horizon behaviour — only a resident process does this).
12	- Control plane **spawns one Execution-coordinator per unit in flight.** Layer 1, a tree walker. Advances work by reading artifacts (§5), never by reading inside a phase; halts on a missing or failed artifact.
13	- The coordinator drives one **planned unit**, drawn as nested containers: **PROJECT ⊃ MILESTONE ⊃ TASK (one issue).**
14	- Inside the task, three **phase spawns** run in sequence, each a Layer 2 skill:
15	  - `exec:build` — goal: produce sliced artifacts (+ `exec:debug`, `exec:simplify`)
16	  - `exec:review` — goal: apply every quality lens (fans out reviewer personas)
17	  - `exec:finish` — goal: land human-readable PRs (What/Why/Focus PR · summary comment · status move)
18	  - Annotate the build→review boundary: **"the agent that produced an artifact never judges it."**
19	- **Review altitudes** sit to the right, each aligned to its container:
20	  - **Task review** — diff-bounded, before the PR merges: spec-compliance · security · reliability/resilience · code-quality · outcome.

22	  - **Project review** — architecture review · measurable stated goals (partial — some goals deferred).
23	- Edge arrows: **work fans down (decomposition)** on the left; **verification rolls up** on the right.

27

29	
30	- **Layer 2 — the workflow pack (skills)** on top: does the work, then leaves signals behind. **WRITES ↓.**

32	- **Layer 1 — the supervisor** below: advances to the next issue, or halts, on whether an artifact exists. **READS ↓.**
33	- Caption: Layer 1 never reads the workflow's steps — only the artifacts it leaves behind; that content-blindness lets the same Layer 2 run under any worker.

margin-top: 6px; }\n  .dg-reads  { font: 600 12px/1 ui-monospace, monospace; color: var(--info); margin-bottom: 4px; }\n  .dg-boundary { margin: 14px 0; padding: 16px 0 4px; border-top: 2.5px dashed var(--warn); }\n  .dg-boundary-label { display: block; text-align: center; font: 600 12px/1 ui-monospace, monospace; color: var(--warn); margin-bottom: 12px; }\n  .dg-chips { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; justify-content: center; gap: 10px; }\n  .dg-chip { padding: 7px 12px; border-radius: 8px; background: var(--warn-soft); border: 1px solid var(--warn); color: var(--fg); font: 600 12.5px/1 ui-monospace, monospace; }\n  .dg-caption { font-size: 13px; color: var(--muted); margin: 16px 0 0; line-height: 1.55; text-align: center; }\n\n  /* dual-mode before/after */\n  .dual { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 16px; margin: 20px 0; }\n  .dual figure { margin: 0;
